text: Almost every near-term quantum algorithm you'll deploy — VQE for chemistry, QAOA for optimization, variational quantum classifiers — is the same loop with different labels on the boxes. Learn this one pattern and you can read, debug, and build the engineering around any of them.

We'll walk the loop step by step, see why it needs a classical optimizer at all, learn to count how many times it'll call the QPU before you ever run it, and see how a convergence check saves real money, not just time.

Here's a real parameterized circuit from IBM Quantum's own documentation. In the variational loop, a circuit shaped like this gets rebuilt with new parameters every single iteration. It's the only step in the whole loop that actually touches quantum hardware.

Spelled out: initialize parameters, build and submit the circuit, execute it on the QPU, compute a cost value from the results, let a classical optimizer propose new parameters, check for convergence, and loop. Count them — six classical steps, one quantum step. The quantum part of a variational algorithm is one line in an otherwise ordinary loop.

This is a real expectation-value plot straight out of IBM's documentation — exactly the kind of number step four extracts from raw measurement counts. That single value is what feeds the cost function, and what the optimizer sees.

Now the arithmetic that actually matters for planning. An eight-parameter circuit using the parameter-shift rule needs seventeen circuit evaluations per iteration. Over a hundred fifty iterations, that's two thousand five hundred fifty evaluations. At a thousand shots each on real IonQ hardware, the full run would cost over seventy-seven thousand dollars. That number is exactly why classical simulators exist — you develop and debug this loop for free, and only point it at real hardware once it's verified correct.

And here's where that loop actually gets built and run in production: Amazon Braket's Hybrid Jobs feature. It's purpose-built to run a classical optimizer driving a quantum circuit as a single managed job — the exact pattern we just walked through.
